title: Numbers 1–20, days and time
summary: Count from 1 to 20 with masculine and feminine nouns, tell the time, name the days of the week and say prices.

sections.body:
Hebrew numbers come in two sets, masculine and feminine, and you choose by the gender of the noun you are counting. The feminine set is also the one for plain counting, phone numbers, bus lines and the time: אחת, שתיים, שלוש… (akhát, shtáyim, shalósh).

From 3 to 10 the endings look “upside down”: the masculine number ends in -ה, which usually marks feminine words, while the feminine number has no ending.
• שלושה ילדים (shloshá yeladím) — three children (ילד is masculine)
• שלוש ילדות (shalósh yeladót) — three girls (ילדה is feminine)

8 is spelled שמונה in both sets; only the stress differs: shmóne (f), shmoná (m). Zero is אפס (éfes).

• 1 comes after the noun and agrees with it, like an adjective: ספר אחד (séfer ekhád) — one book; שאלה אחת (she'elá akhát) — one question.
• 2 has a short form before a noun: שני ספרים (shnei sfarím) — two books; שתי שאלות (shtei she'elót) — two questions. The long forms שניים and שתיים stand on their own: כמה ילדים יש לך? — שניים.
• All the other numbers come before the noun, and the noun is plural: חמישה ספרים, חמש שאלות.

The gender comes from the singular noun, so learn every noun together with its gender: בית (m) → שלושה בתים; כוס (f) → שלוש כוסות; שנה (f) → שלוש שנים, even though שנים ends in -ים.

How many? is כמה? (káma): כמה ילדים יש לכם? — יש לנו שלושה ילדים (How many children do you have? — We have three children).

On the street you will often hear the feminine forms used for everything (“שלוש ילדים”). It's very common in casual speech but counts as a mistake, so learn the standard forms from the start: שלושה ילדים.

11–19 are the unit plus “ten”, and again there are two sets:
• feminine: unit + עשרה (esré) — for counting, the time and feminine nouns: אחת עשרה שעות (eleven hours), שתים עשרה קומות (twelve floors)
• masculine: unit + עשר (asár) — for masculine nouns: אחד עשר שחקנים (eleven players), שמונה עשר שקל (eighteen shekels)

Notice that “ten” swaps too: עשר is the feminine 10 but the masculine ending in 11–19, and עשרה is the masculine 10 but the feminine ending.

12 is usually spelled שתים עשרה and שנים עשר; you will also see שתיים עשרה and שניים עשר. 20, עשרים (esrím), is the same for both genders: עשרים ילדים, עשרים ילדות.

מה השעה? (ma ha-sha'á?) — What time is it? Answer with השעה + a feminine number, because שעה (hour) is feminine: השעה שלוש (ha-sha'á shalósh) — it's three o'clock.

• ו means “and”, i.e. past the hour: שלוש ורבע, שלוש וחצי, שש ועשרים.
• ל means “to”: רבע לארבע (a quarter to four), עשרים לשבע (twenty to seven).
• אחרי (akharéi, after) is another way to say “past”: עשרים אחרי שש = שש ועשרים.
• For 5 and 10 minutes, add דקות (minutes): חמש דקות לשמונה, שבע ועשר דקות. In speech you will also hear them without דקות, in the masculine form: שבע ועשרה, חמישה לשמונה.

To say “at”, attach ב-: באיזו שעה? (be-éyzo sha'á?) — at what time? בשמונה (be-shmóne) — at eight; בשתיים וחצי — at half past two. Add the part of the day when needed: בשבע בבוקר (at seven in the morning), בשלוש אחרי הצהריים, בתשע בערב, באחת בלילה. Timetables and announcements use the 24-hour clock, still with feminine numbers: הרכבת יוצאת בשמונה עשרה ושלושים (The train leaves at 18:30).

The Hebrew days are simply numbered, starting from Sunday, which is the first working day of the Israeli week. Only Saturday has its own name, שבת. Many offices work Sunday to Thursday, and the weekend, סוף שבוע (sof shavú'a), often shortened to סופ״ש, is Friday and Saturday.

“On” a day is ב-: ביום שני (be-yom shení) — on Monday; בשבת — on Saturday. In speech יום is often dropped: נתראה בשלישי (See you on Tuesday).

The days use the ordinal numbers (first, second, third…), not the counting ones: שני in יום שני is shení (second), not shnei (two) — same spelling, different word.

כמה זה עולה? (káma ze olé?) — How much is it? The verb agrees with the thing: כמה עולה החולצה? (How much is the shirt?); כמה עולות הנעליים? (How much are the shoes?)

The shekel, שקל (shékel), is masculine, so prices take the masculine numbers: שני שקלים, חמישה שקלים, שמונה עשר שקל.
• With 2–10 the noun is plural: שלושה שקלים, עשרה שקלים.
• From 11 up, שקל usually stays singular, as a few other very common nouns do (עשרים שנה, twenty years): שמונה עשר שקל (shmoná asár shékel), עשרים שקל.
• שקל or שקל אחד — one shekel; שקל וחצי — one and a half shekels.
• אגורה (agorá, f) is a hundredth of a shekel: עשר אגורות (ten agorot); חצי שקל is fifty agorot.

In speech you will often hear the feminine set here too (“שמונה עשרה שקל”), but the standard form is שמונה עשר שקל. In writing, the sign ₪ or the abbreviation ש״ח (shékel khadásh, “new shekel”) follows the number: 18 ₪, 18 ש״ח.

drills.en: I have three children.
drills.explain: With a masculine noun, 3–10 end in -ה: שלושה ילדים (shloshá yeladím).

drills.en: There are four girls in our class.
drills.explain: With a feminine noun the number has no ending: ארבע בנות (árba banót).

drills.en: I only have one book.
drills.hint: ספר is masculine; 1 comes after the noun
drills.explain: 1 follows the noun and agrees with it like an adjective: ספר אחד (séfer ekhád).

drills.en: I have one question.
drills.explain: שאלה is feminine, so 1 is אחת (akhát): שאלה אחת.

drills.en: There are two rooms in our apartment.
drills.explain: Before a noun, 2 takes its short form: שני (shnei) with masculine nouns. שניים is used only on its own.

drills.en: I drink two cups of coffee a day.
drills.explain: כוס is feminine, so 2 before it is שתי (shtei). שתיים is used only on its own.

drills.en: How many children do you have? — Two.
drills.explain: With no noun after it, 2 takes the long form: שניים (shnáyim), masculine because ילדים is masculine.

drills.en: The notebook costs seven shekels.
drills.explain: שקל is masculine, so 7 is שבעה (shiv'á): שבעה שקלים.

drills.en: What time is it? — Half past three.
drills.hint: the time uses the feminine numbers
drills.explain: שעה is feminine, so the time is told with the feminine (counting) numbers: שלוש וחצי (shalósh ve-khétsi).

drills.en: The meeting is at a quarter past nine.
drills.hint: “at” = ב- attached to a feminine number
drills.explain: “At” a time is ב- + the feminine number: בתשע ורבע (be-tésha ve-réva), 9:15.

drills.en: It's a quarter to eight.
drills.explain: רבע ל- + the next hour means a quarter to: רבע לשמונה (réva le-shmóne) is 7:45.

drills.en: It's twenty past six.
drills.hint: the time uses the feminine numbers
drills.explain: The hour is a feminine number: שש (shesh), not שישה. You can also say שש ועשרים.

drills.en: Today is Friday, and tomorrow is Saturday.
drills.explain: The days are numbered from Sunday, so Friday is יום שישי (yom shishí), “the sixth day”.

drills.en: In Israel the working week starts on Sunday.
drills.explain: Sunday is יום ראשון (yom rishón), “the first day” — the first working day of the Israeli week.

drills.en: Falafel in a pita costs eighteen shekels.
drills.explain: שקל is masculine, so 11–19 take the masculine set ending in עשר: שמונה עשר שקל (shmoná asár shékel). You'll hear שמונה עשרה in the street, but it isn't standard.

drills.en: Our building has twelve floors.
drills.explain: קומה is feminine, so 12 takes the feminine set: שתים עשרה (shtem esré). With a masculine noun it would be שנים עשר.

title: Want to, can, need to: verb + infinitive
summary: Use רוצה, יכול, צריך, אוהב and מתכנן with an infinitive, recognise the shapes of infinitives, and say what is allowed, forbidden, possible or worth doing.

sections.h: Two verbs: the first agrees, the second doesn't
sections.body:
To say “I want to eat” or “she can come”, Hebrew does just what English does: a conjugated verb followed by an infinitive (שם הפועל, shem ha-pó'al). The first verb agrees with the subject; the infinitive never changes.
• אני רוצה לאכול. (aní rotsé le'ekhól) — I (m) want to eat.
• היא רוצה לאכול. (hi rotsá le'ekhól) — She wants to eat.
• הם רוצים לאכול. (hem rotsím le'ekhól) — They want to eat.

In the present tense the first verb has only four forms: masculine or feminine, singular or plural. The pronoun alone doesn't decide: אני and אנחנו take the masculine forms for men and the feminine forms for women, and a mixed group takes the masculine plural.

Word order is simple: subject, conjugated verb, infinitive, then the rest: דנה צריכה לקנות חלב (Dana needs to buy milk).

• רוצה + infinitive — want to: אני רוצה ללמוד עברית (I want to learn Hebrew). With a noun: אני רוצה קפה (I want coffee).
• יכול + infinitive — can, be able to: אתה יכול לעזור לי? (atá yakhól la'azór li?) — Can you help me? This is also the everyday way to ask a favour.
• צריך + infinitive — need to, have to: אני צריכה לעבוד מחר (aní tsrikhá la'avód makhár) — I (f) have to work tomorrow. With a noun it means “need”: אני צריך עזרה (I need help).
• אוהב + infinitive — like or love doing: הם אוהבים לבשל (hem ohavím levashél) — They love cooking. With a noun: אני אוהבת שוקולד.
• מתכנן + infinitive — plan to: אנחנו מתכננים לנסוע לאילת (anákhnu metakhnením linsó'a le-eilát) — We're planning to go to Eilat.
• יודע + infinitive — know how to: היא יודעת לשחות (hi yodá'at liskhót) — She can swim.

Notice that רוצה is spelled the same for a man and a woman; only the pronunciation differs (rotsé / rotsá). In writing, the subject tells you which one is meant.

Almost every infinitive starts with ל-, and its shape tells you a lot about the verb. You don't need the binyanim yet; for now, learn to recognise the patterns:
• Regular pa'al: ל + the root, with ו before the last letter: לכתוב (likhtóv), ללמוד (lilmód), לעבוד (la'avód). When the root ends in ח or ע you hear an extra a at the end: לשמוע (lishmó'a), לפתוח (liftó'akh).
• Roots ending in ה: the ה becomes -ות: לקנות (liknót), לשתות (lishtót), לראות (lir'ót), לעשות (la'asót).
• Roots with ו or י in the middle: just ל + the root: לגור (lagúr), לקום (lakúm), לבוא (lavó), לשים (lasím).
• Short, irregular-looking ones that lose their first root letter and end in ת: לשבת (lashévet), לרדת (larédet), לצאת (latsét), לדעת (ladá'at), לתת (latét, which loses both נs of נ.ת.ן). Learn these as words.
• Infinitives starting with le- + a stem, or with לה-, belong to the other binyanim: לדבר (ledabér), להבין (lehavín), להתקשר (lehitkashér), להיכנס (lehikanés).
table: ל + root, ו before the last letter (pa'al)
root ends in ח or ע
ו or י in the middle
short forms ending in ת (first letter gone)

sections.h: One form for everyone: אסור, מותר, אפשר, כדאי
sections.body:
These words never change for gender or number. Followed by an infinitive, they state a rule or a possibility for everyone, which makes them ideal for signs, rules and polite questions:
• אסור (asúr) — it's forbidden: אסור לעשן כאן. — Smoking is not allowed here.
• מותר (mutár) — it's allowed: מותר להיכנס עם כלב? — Can you come in with a dog?
• אפשר (efshár) — it's possible, one can: אפשר לשלם בכרטיס? — Can I pay by card?
• כדאי (kedái) — it's worth it, it's a good idea: כדאי לבוא מוקדם. — It's a good idea to come early.
• צריך can work the same way, with no subject: צריך לקנות חלב. — We need to buy milk.

To say who, add ל- with a personal ending: אסור לי לאכול סוכר (I'm not allowed to eat sugar), כדאי לך לנסות (You should try it), מותר לנו לשבת כאן? (Are we allowed to sit here?).

לא goes before the verb that agrees with the subject:
• אני לא יכול לבוא היום. (aní lo yakhól lavó ha-yóm) — I (m) can't come today.
• היא לא רוצה לאכול. — She doesn't want to eat.
• הם לא אוהבים לחכות. — They don't like waiting.

With the one-form words:
• לא כדאי — it's not a good idea: לא כדאי לנסוע עכשיו, יש פקקים (It's not a good idea to drive now; there are traffic jams).
• לא צריך — there's no need: לא צריך לשלם, זה בחינם (No need to pay, it's free).
• אי אפשר (i efshár) — it's impossible, you can't; never ✗ לא אפשר: אי אפשר לחנות כאן (You can't park here).

Careful: לא צריך means “you don't have to”, but אסור means “you mustn't”. “You don't have to come” is לא צריך לבוא; אסור לבוא would mean you are forbidden to come.

לא can also stand before the infinitive, negating only the second verb: כדאי לא לשכוח את הדרכון (Better not to forget your passport). On signs, a bare infinitive gives the instruction: לא לעשן (No smoking), לא לגעת (Do not touch).

drills.en: She wants to learn Hebrew.
drills.explain: רוצה is spelled the same for a man and a woman (rotsé / rotsá); the infinitive ללמוד doesn't change.

drills.en: Dana, can you help me?
drills.explain: יכול agrees with the subject: את → יכולה (yekholá). The infinitive לעזור stays the same.

drills.prompt: יוסי ___ לעבוד היום עד שש. (need to)
drills.en: Yossi needs to work until six today.
drills.explain: יוסי is a man, so צריך (tsaríkh); the infinitive לעבוד never changes.

drills.en: My daughters love to dance.
drills.explain: אוהב agrees with הבנות, feminine plural: אוהבות (ohavót).

drills.prompt: מיכל ואנה ___ לנסוע לאילת בקיץ. (plan to)
drills.en: Michal and Anna are planning to go to Eilat in the summer.
drills.explain: Two women take the feminine plural: מתכננות (metakhnenót). With even one man in the group it would be מתכננים.

drills.en: You need to write an email to the manager.
drills.hint: pa'al: ל + root, with ו before the last letter
drills.explain: כ.ת.ב → לכתוב (likhtóv): ל + the root, with ו before the last letter.

drills.en: I want to buy a new computer.
drills.explain: Roots ending in ה form the infinitive with -ות: ק.נ.ה → לקנות (liknót).

drills.en: We want to live near the sea.
drills.explain: ג.ו.ר has ו in the middle, so the infinitive is simply ל + the root: לגור (lagúr).

drills.en: The children don't want to sit quietly.
drills.explain: י.ש.ב has a short infinitive without its first letter: לשבת (lashévet), like לרדת and לצאת.

drills.prompt: אני לא יכולה ___ אותו, הוא מדבר מהר מדי. (to understand)
drills.en: I can't understand him; he talks too fast.
drills.explain: להבין (lehavín) has the hif'il shape: לה- + the stem, with י before the last letter, like להזמין. It never changes, whoever the subject is.

drills.en: You're not allowed to talk on the phone in the library.
drills.explain: אסור (asúr) + infinitive = it's forbidden. It never changes for gender or number.

drills.en: Is it OK to sit here?
drills.explain: מותר (mutár) + infinitive = it's allowed. Like אסור, it has only one form.

drills.prompt: ___ לקבל עוד כוס מים? (is it possible)
drills.en: Could I have another glass of water?
drills.explain: אפשר (efshár) + infinitive is the standard polite way to ask for something: אפשר לקבל…?

drills.prompt: ___ לקחת מטרייה, היום יורד גשם. (it's a good idea)
drills.en: It's a good idea to take an umbrella; it's raining today.
drills.explain: כדאי (kedái) + infinitive = it's worth it, it's a good idea. It never changes.

drills.prompt: אני ___ לבוא למסיבה, אני עובד בערב. (can't)
drills.en: I can't come to the party; I'm working in the evening.
drills.explain: לא goes before the verb that agrees with the subject: לא יכול (lo yakhól). The speaker is a man (אני עובד).

drills.prompt: אתם ___ להביא אוכל, יש הרבה. (don't need to)
drills.en: You don't need to bring food; there's plenty.
drills.explain: לא צריכים = you don't have to. אסור would mean you are forbidden to bring food.

title: The past tense of pa'al
summary: Build the past of pa'al verbs with the endings every binyan shares, put the stress in the right place, and handle common weak verbs such as היה, בא, ישב and נתן.

sections.body:
The past tense (עבר, avár) is a stem plus an ending that shows the person. In pa'al the stem is simply the three root letters: ל.מ.ד → למד (lamád), “he studied”. The הוא form has no ending at all, and it's the form under which verbs are listed in Hebrew dictionaries.

These endings are worth learning perfectly, because they are exactly the same in every binyan: דיברתי (I talked), הזמנתי (I invited) and התקשרתי (I phoned) all end in -תי, just like למדתי.

Since the ending already shows the person, אני, אתה, את, אנחנו, אתם and אתן are often left out: למדתי = I studied, גמרנו = we finished. With הוא, היא, הם and הן you normally say who: הוא למד, דנה למדה, הילדים למדו.

sections.h: Stress, and כתבת for both אתה and את
sections.body:
Where the stress falls is part of the form:
• With -תי, -ת and -נו the stress stays on the stem: lamádti, lamádta, lamádnu.
• With -ה and -ו the stem's second vowel drops and the stress moves to the ending: lamdá, lamdú. So היא למדה (lamdá, she studied) sounds quite different from the present היא לומדת (lomédet, she studies).
• For אתם / אתן the textbook form is lmadtém, stressed on the ending; in everyday speech almost everyone says lamádtem. The same split holds for every verb in this lesson: the tables below give the everyday forms (kanítem, bátem, natátem), while the textbook ones stress the ending (knitém, batém, netatém).

אתה and את share one written form: כתבת is katávta (you, m.) or katávt (you, f.). You hear the difference; in writing, the context or the pronoun tells you: אתה כתבת את המייל? / את כתבת את המייל? (Did you write the email?) In the second sentence the first את is “you” and the second is the object marker.

One more pair to watch: כתבה is both katvá, “she wrote”, and katavá, “an article”: היא כתבה כתבה על העיר (She wrote an article about the city).

Verbs whose root ends in ה are among the most common in the language: להיות (to be), לקנות (to buy), לשתות (to drink), לראות (to see), לעשות (to do). Their past has three twists:
• Before -תי, -ת, -נו, -תם and -תן the ה becomes י: קניתי (kaníti), ראינו (ra'ínu).
• With היא the ה becomes ת, and then -ה is added: קנתה (kantá), שתתה (shatetá), הייתה (haytá).
• With הם / הן the ה simply drops: קנו (kanú), היו (hayú).

להיות is spelled with a double י in most forms: הייתי, היית, הייתה, היינו, הייתם. It gives the past of sentences that have no verb in the present: אני בבית → הייתי בבית; הוא עייף → הוא היה עייף (he was tired).

It also turns יש לי into the past. Here היה agrees with the thing you have, not with the person: היה לי יום ארוך (m.), הייתה לי פגישה (f.), היו לי שאלות (pl.). In the negative, אין לי becomes לא היה לי / לא הייתה לי / לא היו לי.

Roots with ו or י in the middle (ב.ו.א, ק.ו.ם, ג.ו.ר, ש.י.ם) lose that letter in the past, so the stem has only two letters: בא, קם, גר, שם. The endings are the usual ones, but the stress stays on the stem, even with -ה and -ו: gárti, gára, gáru (only the textbook אתם / אתן forms, gartém, gartén, stress the ending).

In the third person singular the past and the present are written the same: הוא גר is “he lives” or “he lived”, and היא גרה is gará in the present but gára in the past. Time words remove the doubt: אתמול הוא בא מאוחר (Yesterday he came late). In the plural there's no confusion: הם גרים (they live), הם גרו (they lived).

In בא the א is silent: באתי (báti), באנו (bánu), באו (bá'u).

sections.h: Verbs beginning with י or נ: ישב, ירד, נסע, נתן
sections.body:
In the infinitive and the future some verbs lose their first root letter (לשבת, לרדת, לתת; אשב, אסע), which makes them look irregular. The good news: in the past they are completely regular, and the first letter is back: ישבתי (yashávti), ירדנו (yarádnu), נסעתי (nasáti), נסעו (nas'ú).

The one real twist is נתן (to give). Its last root letter is נ, and before an ending that starts with ת it merges with that ת: נתתי (natáti), נתת (natáta / natát), נתתם (natátem). Notice, too, that נתנו is both natánu, “we gave”, and natnú, “they gave”.

sections.h: When? Time words for the past
sections.body:
• אתמול (etmól) — yesterday; שלשום (shilshóm) — the day before yesterday
• הבוקר (ha-bóker) — this morning; אתמול בערב — yesterday evening, last night
• לפני (lifnéi) + a period of time = ago: לפני שבוע (a week ago), לפני חודש, לפני שלוש שנים, לפני שנתיים (two years ago), לפני רגע (a moment ago)
• בשבוע שעבר (ba-shavú'a she-avár) — last week; בחודש שעבר — last month; בשנה שעברה (ba-shaná she-avrá) — last year
• כבר (kvar) — already; עוד לא (od lo) — not yet: כבר אכלתי. / עוד לא אכלתי.

שעבר is ש- (that) + עבר, itself a pa'al past verb meaning “passed”. So it agrees like any verb: שבוע and חודש are masculine (שעבר), שנה is feminine (שעברה).

Time words usually open the sentence, and לא goes straight before the verb: אתמול לא נסענו לחיפה, נשארנו בבית (Yesterday we didn't go to Haifa; we stayed at home).

drills.en: Yesterday I studied for three hours.
drills.explain: Past with אני adds -תי to the stem: למדתי (lamádti).

drills.prompt: רונית ___ את החלון, כי היה קר. (לסגור)
drills.en: Ronit closed the window because it was cold.
drills.explain: היא adds -ה and the stem's second vowel drops: סגרה (sagrá).

drills.en: We sat in a café by the sea.
drills.hint: the י of the root is back in the past
drills.explain: In the past ישב is regular, first letter included: ישבנו (yashávnu).

drills.en: David, did you see the new film?
drills.explain: ראה is a final-heh verb, so the ה becomes י: ראית (ra'íta). את ראית (ra'ít) is written the same.

drills.en: They got off the bus at the central bus station.
drills.explain: The past of לרדת has its י back: ירדו (yardú).

drills.prompt: בשבוע שעבר ___ לאילת עם המשפחה. (לנסוע, אני)
drills.en: Last week I went to Eilat with my family.
drills.hint: the נ of the root is there in the past
drills.explain: נסעתי (nasáti): the נ that disappears in the future (אסע) is part of the past stem.

drills.prompt: מירב ___ בירושלים חמש שנים, ואחר כך עברה לחיפה. (לגור)
drills.en: Merav lived in Jerusalem for five years and then moved to Haifa.
drills.explain: Hollow verbs have a two-letter stem: גרה (gára). The present גרה is written the same but said gará; here עברה (moved) shows that it's the past.

drills.en: Did you get up early this morning?
drills.explain: Two-letter stem + -תם: קמתם (kámtem in everyday speech; textbook kamtém).

drills.en: The guests came at eight in the evening.
drills.explain: בא + -ו = באו (bá'u); in hollow verbs the stress stays on the stem.

drills.prompt: אתמול ___ חולה, אז לא באתי לשיעור. (להיות, אני)
drills.en: Yesterday I was sick, so I didn't come to class.
drills.explain: להיות is a final-heh verb: הייתי (hayíti), written with a double י.

drills.en: What did you buy at the supermarket yesterday?
drills.explain: The ה becomes י before -ת: קנית (kanít), written exactly like אתה קנית (kaníta).

drills.en: She drank two cups of coffee this morning.
drills.explain: With היא the ה turns into ת before -ה: שתתה (shatetá), like קנתה and הייתה.

drills.en: Yesterday I had an important meeting.
drills.explain: יש לי becomes היה / הייתה / היו לי, agreeing with the thing you had: פגישה is feminine, so הייתה (haytá).

drills.en: I gave him my number.
drills.hint: the last נ of the root merges with the ending
drills.explain: נ.ת.ן + -תי: the final נ merges with the ת of the ending, giving נתתי (natáti).

drills.en: A month ago we moved to a new apartment.
drills.explain: לפני + a period of time means “ago”: לפני חודש (lifnéi khódesh).

drills.en: We got married last year.
drills.hint: עבר agrees with שנה, which is feminine
drills.explain: בשנה שעברה (ba-shaná she-avrá): עבר is a past verb, “that passed”, so it agrees with the feminine שנה. With שבוע it's בשבוע שעבר.
